thread_analysis.thread_summary: NEC Platforms (contact Hidemasa Hashimoto, with several CC'd colleagues) engages Allion (Itsuo Sakai, Masaya Iida) for Bluetooth SIG registration of LCD communication terminal products, spanning February through April 2026. The thread is exceptionally instructive for post-registration My Page interface interpretation, covering TCW's separate approval process and a detailed, multi-round clarification of the alarming-but-benign 'Withdraw Product' UI element.
all_questions_found: What happens after Submission when a TCW is involved, and who receives the approval/rejection notification? (see thread_0050_case_01)
How can a registrant confirm registration completion via My Page, and what does the '×Withdraw Product' label next to a product listing actually mean? (see thread_0050_case_02)

(Administrative, not separately cased) Standard quote/Invoice/payment timeline including Taiwan HQ internal approval and Lunar New Year holiday accommodation, Compliance Folder document submission for a representative model among multiple SKU variants (consistent with already-documented representative-model flexibility), and detailed invoice/bank-transfer formatting instructions for the customer's accounting process.
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: Case_01's clarification that TCW applications undergo a separate SIG-side approval/rejection process (1-5 business days) with direct registrant notification is a valuable procedural detail. Case_02 is an unusually thorough, multi-round (three separate emails) clarification of a confusing UI element that this thread documents in more depth than anywhere else in the corpus -- including the underlying anti-gaming rationale for why SIG deliberately avoids letting Listing Owners directly edit Product List entries.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: See thread_0050_case_01 and thread_0050_case_02 for case-specific decision logic.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: See individual case files; case_02's risk is particularly salient given how persistently the customer remained confused across three separate follow-up emails despite repeated explanation, underscoring how genuinely counterintuitive this UI element is.
thread_analysis.consulting_mistake: None identified -- the consultant patiently re-explained the Withdraw Product mechanism across multiple rounds of customer confusion, eventually providing the underlying design rationale (anti-gaming prevention) that finally fully resolved the customer's concern.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: When a customer is confused by a SIG interface element that looks alarming but is actually benign (like the 'Withdraw Product' label appearing mechanically on every Product List entry), don't stop at a single explanation -- be prepared to explain the underlying design rationale if initial clarifications don't fully resolve the customer's concern, since some SIG UI choices are non-intuitive by deliberate design (to prevent gaming of the unregistered-product detection process) rather than simple oversights.
